strengths: The paper investigates a worthwhile direction: learning text-aligned visual embeddings directly from compact Gaussian parameters. Adapting this representation to CLIP on 12.8M DataComp pairs provides a meaningful feasibility study beyond reconstruction or supervised classification.

Figure 6 demonstrates substantial semantic retention: approximately 13–15% zero-shot ImageNet top-1 accuracy versus 18.5% for the RGB baseline, with relatively stable performance across intermediate splat counts. Surpassing RGB accuracy is not necessary for this contribution to be useful.

The batched fitting implementation offers potentially valuable infrastructure. Figure 2 reports substantial speedups across multiple batch sizes, reaching 90.3×, while structured initialization produces markedly better reconstructions in the illustrated example.

The manuscript acknowledges the accuracy gap and reports unsuccessful training from scratch. Comparing 98 versus 196 resampled tokens also provides useful evidence about the capacity–accuracy tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central efficiency proposition is not established against practical alternatives. The reported 3–23.5× compression compares float16 Gaussian parameters with uncompressed pixels, without matched-byte JPEG or other codec baselines. There are no end-to-end latency, energy, or memory measurements accounting for iterative fitting and resampling. Processing 400–3136 splats into 98 or 196 tokens does not itself demonstrate lower compute than processing 196 RGB patches. These missing comparisons materially limit the claimed deployment advantage.

The experiments do not isolate representation loss from adaptation limitations. An RGB encoder evaluated on rendered Gaussian reconstructions would reveal how much of the accuracy gap comes from compression versus the splat encoder. A comparable RGB resampling or reduced-resolution baseline is also absent. Moreover, the claim of identical training conditions is misleading: RGB receives 32 epochs, whereas Gaussian adaptation inherits that checkpoint and receives six additional epochs with different trainable components.

The algorithmic contributions receive insufficient validation. Structured initialization is supported by one illustrated image at a fixed iteration count, which cannot establish higher asymptotic quality. Pruning is likewise illustrated on one image, without aggregate reconstruction results or downstream accuracy ablations. The assumption that low luminance implies low semantic information is unjustified; dark regions can contain important objects and boundaries.

The systems results lack absolute fitting throughput or latency, memory consumption, and reconstruction quality under the timed settings. The headline speedup uses batch size 4096, so its relevance to individual edge-device inputs is unclear. Although the batching improvement is promising, the reported ratios do not establish practical encoding cost or disentangle the system and algorithmic improvements.

Reproducibility is limited by missing fitting optimizer settings, pruning coefficients and schedules, Fourier frequencies, stem dimensions, resampler depth and attention configuration, and precise data preprocessing. The covariance log transformation is not specified sufficiently to understand its handling of signed entries. The claimed 7% trainable fraction also lacks a parameter breakdown despite unfreezing two transformer blocks and adding a trainable stem/resampler; code is only promised.

Evaluation supports a narrower conclusion than general multimodal usefulness: ImageNet classification is the sole downstream task, and its validation set is also used to select the RGB checkpoint. No retrieval or independent transfer evaluation corroborates generalization. Separately, Figure 7(b) is labeled as top-5 accuracy but displays training loss, duplicating panel (c); this is a correctable reporting error. Overall, the feasibility contribution is worthwhile, but the unresolved efficiency comparisons and attribution gaps currently favor weak rejection.

strengths: The paper explores a worthwhile alternative to pixel-based vision–language alignment: directly encoding Gaussian parameters. Training on 12.8M DataComp pairs provides a substantive feasibility study beyond small supervised classification experiments.

Figure 6 demonstrates useful semantic transfer: Gaussian encoders achieve approximately 13–15% zero-shot ImageNet top-1 accuracy versus 18.5% for the RGB baseline. Performance changes moderately across several splat budgets, and the 98-token variant establishes a concrete accuracy–token-count trade-off.

Batched fitting is a potentially useful systems contribution. Figure 2 reports speedups across multiple batch sizes and two splat configurations, reaching 90.3×. Structured initialization also produces visibly better reconstruction than random initialization at a fixed iteration budget.
The manuscript acknowledges the accuracy gap, unsuccessful training from scratch, and absence of codec-side quantization rather than claiming superior recognition performance.
weaknesses: The central practical efficiency claim is not established. The reported 3–23.5× compression compares float16 Gaussian parameters with raw pixels, without matched-byte comparisons against JPEG or other conventional codecs. No end-to-end latency, energy, or memory measurements account for iterative Gaussian fitting and the additional resampler. Consequently, the accuracy loss is not accompanied by a demonstrated advantage over realistic image-transmission pipelines.

The experiments do not isolate why direct Gaussian encoding is useful. Missing controls include applying the RGB encoder to rendered Gaussian reconstructions, comparing compressed or downsampled RGB at similar storage budgets, and using an RGB resampler at the same token count. These comparisons would distinguish representation loss, encoder adaptation difficulty, and generic token reduction.

Evidence for the algorithmic contributions is limited. Structured initialization is illustrated on one image at 3,000 iterations; this does not establish the claimed higher asymptotic quality. Luminance pruning is illustrated on another image without aggregate reconstruction results or downstream accuracy ablations. Low luminance is not a reliable proxy for low semantic importance, and the claimed preservation of semantic content remains untested.

The systems results lack absolute fitting throughput, per-image latency, memory requirements, and quality-matched timing comparisons. The headline 90.3× result uses a batch of 4,096 images, making its relevance to resource-constrained edge encoding uncertain. GPU utilization alone does not establish computational or energy efficiency.

Architectural and training details are insufficient for reliable reproduction: Fourier frequencies, resampler depth and dimensions, covariance log transformation, fitting schedules, and pruning settings used for alignment are not fully specified. The reported 7% trainable-parameter fraction lacks an explicit parameter breakdown despite unfreezing two transformer blocks and training additional modules. Code is promised but not supplied in the manuscript.

Some reporting issues further weaken interpretation. Claims of identical training conditions overlook the distinction between 32-epoch RGB pretraining and six-epoch Gaussian adaptation from that checkpoint. ImageNet validation is used for checkpoint selection and final reporting, with no independent transfer evaluation. Figure 7(b), captioned as top-5 accuracy, instead repeats the training-loss plot; this is a correctable presentation error.

Overall, the feasibility result and batching work have merit, but the missing practical baselines and contribution-specific validation leave the main efficiency and methodological claims insufficiently supported. These concerns, rather than the lack of state-of-the-art accuracy alone, determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper investigates a worthwhile alternative to pixel-based vision–language learning: directly aligning compact Gaussian image representations with text. Extending this approach to 12.8M DataComp image–text pairs is a useful exploratory contribution.

The adaptation pipeline demonstrates that Gaussian parameters retain transferable semantic information. Figure 6 reports roughly 13–15% ImageNet zero-shot top-1 accuracy versus 18.5% for the RGB baseline, with relatively stable performance across several splat budgets.

The batched CUDA implementation offers potentially valuable infrastructure. Figure 2 reports substantial throughput improvements across multiple batch sizes and Gaussian counts, reaching 90.3× over the cited implementation.

Reusing an RGB-pretrained transformer through a splat-aware stem and Perceiver resampler is technically plausible. The manuscript acknowledges the accuracy gap and reports unsuccessful training-from-scratch results, providing useful context.
weaknesses: The central practical efficiency advantage remains unestablished. The reported 3–23.5× compression compares float16 Gaussian parameters with raw pixels, rather than transmitted JPEG or another codec at matched recognition accuracy. No end-to-end encoding, transmission, inference latency, or energy measurements are provided. Consequently, the experiments do not establish the claimed edge–cloud benefit.

The evaluation does not isolate the value of the Gaussian representation or the proposed architecture. There are no matched-byte compressed/downsampled RGB controls, RGB token-reduction controls, or comparisons with rendering the same splats and applying the RGB encoder. Ablations of the Fourier encoding, covariance processing, gating, and resampler are absent. These omissions prevent identifying whether the accuracy loss comes from compression or adaptation and whether the proposed components are necessary.

The systems results lack absolute fitting times, throughput, memory requirements, and clearly documented matched-quality comparisons. The largest speedup uses a batch of 4096 images; this establishes a batching opportunity but does not demonstrate efficient individual-image encoding on an edge device. Likewise, halving transformer tokens does not establish a net compute saving without accounting for cross-attention over 400–3136 splats.

The algorithmic fitting contributions have limited quantitative support. Structured initialization is illustrated on one image at a fixed iteration count, which does not establish the claimed higher asymptotic quality. Luminance-based pruning is illustrated qualitatively without dataset-level reconstruction or downstream accuracy ablations. Low luminance is not generally evidence of low semantic importance.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript omits important fitting hyperparameters, pruning schedules and thresholds, resampler configuration, Fourier frequencies, and precise normalization/log-scaling definitions. The stated 7% trainable-parameter fraction lacks a parameter breakdown despite unfreezing two transformer blocks and adding a stem. Figure 7(b) also duplicates a training-loss plot while being labeled top-5 accuracy; this is a correctable presentation error.

Overall, the demonstrated semantic transfer and batching improvements are worthwhile, and failure to match RGB accuracy is not itself grounds for rejection. However, the missing efficiency comparisons and component-level evidence leave the main contribution insufficiently substantiated, favoring weak rejection.

strengths: The paper provides a worthwhile large-scale feasibility study of direct vision–language alignment from Gaussian image representations. Processing 12.8M image–text pairs and evaluating across diverse zero-shot datasets extends prior Gaussian recognition work beyond supervised classification.

The adaptation pipeline is technically plausible and supported by architectural studies. Figures 14–19 compare distillation strategies, normalization, alternative stems, and point transformers, supporting the combination of RGB distillation and a Perceiver stem.

The results demonstrate substantial preservation of recognition information: the 1600-point model achieves 20.31 mean accuracy versus 22.20 for RGB, with a representation 5.88 times smaller than uncompressed pixels. Some datasets, including Cars and SUN397, improve over the teacher baseline.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, per-dataset results, adapted RGB baselines, and negative findings on training from scratch. Batched fitting and structured initialization are potentially useful engineering contributions independently of the broader deployment claims.
weaknesses: The central practical compression advantage is not established against realistic transmission baselines. Table 1 compares FP16 splats exclusively with uncompressed RGB, although the introduction explicitly motivates replacing JPEG-based transmission. There is no matched-byte comparison against JPEG/WebP or lower-resolution RGB with downstream accuracy measured. The reported 3–23.5× ratios therefore demonstrate compactness relative to raw pixels, but do not establish an advantageous communication–accuracy tradeoff.

End-to-end efficiency remains unmeasured. Data loading and decoding times exclude iterative Gaussian fitting and encoder execution. The GS stem adds four cross-attention layers over 400–3136 primitives, so reducing the subsequent transformer to 98 tokens does not itself establish lower total computation. No complete latency, memory, or energy comparison supports the edge–cloud efficiency claims, and the offline H100 preprocessing setup does not demonstrate practical edge encoding.

The systems evidence contains a consequential accounting error. In Table 3, the reported 'Speedup' equals batch fitting time divided by single-image fitting time: 13/7 = 1.86 for batch size 128. Throughput speedup would instead be 128×7/13, approximately 68.9×. Additionally, the fraction of active GPU time spent in kernels does not establish the claimed 97% GPU utilization. These issues do not negate the batching benefit, but weaken confidence in a headline contribution and require reconciliation with Figure 2.

The headline accuracy-retention metric gives an overly favorable picture of useful recognition preservation. The 3136-point model's 0.98 average relative accuracy corresponds to 20.39/22.20, approximately 92%, when comparing mean absolute accuracy. Dataset-wise ratios can be inflated by improvements near chance, such as dSprites y-position increasing from 1.88% to 3.18%. Meanwhile, substantial failures include diabetic retinopathy declining from 38.33% to 3.09% and ObjectNet from 19.99% to 14.64%. Both metrics are disclosed, but the broad claim of retaining 96–98% of RGB accuracy needs stronger qualification.

The token-reduction comparison does not isolate an advantage of Gaussian representations. Table 1 foregrounds an unadapted RGB merging baseline, whereas Table 7 shows that five epochs of RGB adaptation achieve 20.56 mean accuracy at 98 tokens, exceeding every reported 98-token GS model. The highest relative-ratio score slightly favors GS, but a matched RGB Perceiver or comparable learned pooling baseline is absent.

The pruning contribution is disconnected from the alignment results: Section 6 confirms that all main models use unpruned representations. Reconstruction PSNR alone cannot establish preservation of semantic information after luminance-based pruning. More broadly, the strongest supported contribution is a promising representation-transfer study; the missing practical baselines and unreliable efficiency accounting concern its central claimed benefit, rather than merely evaluation breadth or presentation, and determine my weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper makes a worthwhile contribution by demonstrating vision–language alignment directly from Gaussian parameters at the scale of 12.8M image–text pairs. Extending Gaussian image representations to this setting is useful even without outperforming RGB encoders.

The adaptation pipeline is technically plausible and reasonably documented: Fourier features, covariance normalization, a Perceiver resampler, RGB-feature distillation, and selective CLIP fine-tuning. The appendix provides meaningful comparisons of initialization, distillation objectives, stems, normalization, and training from scratch.

The results establish substantial semantic retention. For example, GS-1600 achieves 16.87% ImageNet accuracy versus 18.51% for RGB, and 74.35% versus 75.17% on STL-10. Its average accuracy changes only from 20.31% to 20.07% when reducing latent tokens from 196 to 98.

Batched Gaussian fitting is potentially useful infrastructure. The paper supplies profiling results, reconstruction studies, and preprocessing configurations, and explicitly acknowledges fitting costs, dependence on RGB pretraining, and the absence of pruning in the alignment experiments.
weaknesses: The central practical compression claim lacks the relevant comparison. The reported 3–23.5× ratios are against uncompressed RGB bytes, although the motivating edge–cloud setting ordinarily transmits compressed images. There is no accuracy-versus-transmitted-bytes comparison with JPEG or another practical codec. Table 1's loading/decoding measurements also do not establish network savings or end-to-end efficiency, particularly after including iterative Gaussian fitting. This leaves a major claimed advantage unresolved.

The headline token-reduction comparison uses an inadequately adapted RGB baseline. GS models receive distillation and five epochs of CLIP adaptation, whereas the main 98-token RGB result uses averaging without fine-tuning. The stronger baseline is available in Table 7: five-epoch RGB fine-tuning reaches 20.56% average accuracy, exceeding every 98-token GS variant, and 0.95 relative accuracy versus GS's best 0.96. Thus, the appendix substantially narrows the apparent advantage. No encoder latency or memory measurements account for the four additional cross-attention layers over 400–3136 splats.

The advertised 96–98% accuracy retention relies on averaging dataset-wise ratios, which can emphasize gains on tasks with very low baseline accuracy. Table 5 instead gives 20.39% average accuracy for GS-3136 versus 22.20% for RGB, approximately 92% retention by the ratio of means. Important failures are also obscured by the aggregate: diabetic-retinopathy accuracy falls from 38.33% to 3.09%, and FER2013 from 17.41% to 7.19%. The metric is defined, but the broad robustness interpretation is stronger than these results support.

The systems evidence contains concrete reporting problems. Table 3's 'Speedup' values equal batch time divided by single-image time: 327/7 = 46.71, whereas throughput speedup at batch size 4096 would be approximately 87.7×. Its kernel percentages describe fractions of active GPU time and do not independently substantiate 97% GPU utilization. Table 4's stated GPU-hour calculation is also dimensionally incorrect. These issues do not negate batching benefits, but weaken confidence in a principal quantitative contribution.

The pruning contribution is disconnected from the demonstrated alignment results: all CLIP experiments use unpruned splats. Reconstruction PSNR alone therefore does not establish that luminance pruning preserves semantic information. More broadly, the architectural ingredients are mostly established techniques, making the quality of the empirical efficiency comparison particularly important. The useful feasibility demonstration is presently outweighed by the unresolved codec comparison, baseline imbalance, and systems-reporting issues; these determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper investigates a worthwhile representation question: whether Gaussian parameters can directly support vision–language alignment without rasterization. Scaling this investigation to 12.8M image–text pairs is a meaningful extension beyond the smaller supervised settings discussed in related work.

The adaptation pipeline is technically plausible and empirically useful. RGB-feature distillation, a Perceiver stem, and selective backbone tuning allow substantial reuse of pretrained models. At 1600 splats, ImageNet accuracy reaches 16.87% versus 18.51% for the RGB teacher while using 5.88× fewer bytes than uncompressed RGB.

The appendix contains useful architectural and training studies. Comparisons against alternative stems, joint distillation, scratch training, and rendered Gaussian images help explain why the proposed recipe works and identify remaining architectural limitations.

Batched Gaussian fitting and structured initialization have practical value for dataset preparation. The paper also candidly acknowledges offline fitting costs, dependence on RGB pretraining, and the fact that pruning is not used in the final alignment experiments.
weaknesses: The central transmission-efficiency claim lacks the relevant comparison. All reported compression ratios use uncompressed RGB as the denominator, although the introduction explicitly motivates replacing JPEG-based transmission. There is no measured accuracy-versus-bytes comparison against JPEG or another practical codec, or even reduced-resolution RGB. Table 1 measures loading and decoding rather than network transfer or complete inference, and its storage, caching, and decoding conditions are insufficiently specified. Thus the experiments establish compactness relative to raw pixels, but not the claimed practical advantage for edge–cloud systems. This is a principal reason for my weak-reject recommendation.

The headline accuracy-retention figures overstate the strength of the demonstrated alignment. The 98% figure for GS-3136 is an average of dataset-wise ratios; its mean absolute accuracy is 20.39% versus 22.20%, approximately 92% of the baseline mean. Ratios on tasks with near-chance performance can contribute disproportionately: dSprites y-position rises from 1.88% to 3.18%, approximately chance for 32 classes. Meanwhile, diabetic-retinopathy accuracy falls from 38.33% to 3.09%, FER2013 from 17.41% to 7.19%, and ObjectNet from 19.99% to 14.64%. Reporting both metrics is transparent, but the broad semantic-preservation claims need more qualification. The issue is not failure to achieve state of the art; it is that weak baseline competence on many tasks limits what relative retention establishes.

The token-efficiency comparison does not isolate a Gaussian-specific advantage. The main 98-token RGB baseline merges tokens without adaptation, whereas the GS models receive distillation and subsequent training. Table 7 shows that five epochs of RGB adaptation recover 20.56% mean accuracy, exceeding every 98-token GS model in Table 5. Moreover, the GS stem introduces four cross-attention layers over 400–3136 primitives. Without end-to-end latency, memory, or FLOP measurements, fewer backbone tokens do not establish lower total computation.

The systems evidence contains a concrete numerical error. Table 3 labels the ratio of batch latency to single-image latency as 'Speedup': 13/7 = 1.86 for batch size 128, whereas throughput speedup from those timings would be 128×7/13 ≈ 68.9. Similarly, 327/7 = 46.71 is reported for batch size 4096. This does not independently disprove Figure 2, but it makes the supporting performance accounting unreliable. The fraction of active GPU time spent in kernels also does not, by itself, establish 97% overall GPU utilization.

The pruning contribution is disconnected from the main learning results: every final alignment model uses unpruned parameters. Its reconstruction-only experiments therefore do not establish preservation of downstream semantics. In addition, color magnitude alone ignores Gaussian spatial extent and overlap, so its interpretation as information density is heuristic rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite helpful architectural details. The manuscript does not clearly specify the fitting optimizer and learning rate, stage-specific adaptation hyperparameters, augmentation handling for offline splats, or which reported models use optional text-side unfreezing. Code is promised rather than supplied, and no run-to-run uncertainty is reported. These omissions particularly affect confidence in small differences among configurations.
